newsitem.title: SPAIN: NATO's Solana to help Spain into military command.
newsitem.headline: NATO's Solana to help Spain into military command.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana met Spanish leaders on Monday and promised to throw all his weight behind Madrid to help it join the Atlantic alliance's military structure.

"I will try to bring about the conditions Spain seeks for its full integration. I have a feeling it will be possible," Solana, a former Spanish foreign minister, said after meeting Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar and other senior officials.

Spain, a member of the 16-nation NATO but not of its integrated military command, says it will join the alliance's military structure on condition it can host a NATO command controlling access to the Mediterranean and all of Iberia.
Foreign Minister Abel Matutes told a joint news conference with Solana this condition was put forth in negotiations on Spain's probable integration into the alliance command.

"...one of the conditions Spain wants to see satisfied in this negotiation is for an operative command to exist in Spain over the straits (of Gibraltar) and all of the Iberian peninsula," Matutes said.

Spain's demand clashes with Portugal's proposal for Spain, France and Portugal to rotate in a regional, Lisbon-based command over the Gibraltar Straits -- the Atlantic Ocean gateway to the Mediterranean.
Britain, on the other hand, is wary of Spain's claims to sovereignty over the tiny colony of Gibraltar, ruled from London for nearly three centuries.
But Madrid now hopes Britain and Portugal will drop their resistance to seeing it take a role in the NATO command.

"The strategic situation in the world has changed radically and therefore I think that now neither the United Kingdom nor of course Portugal will oppose Spain taking responsibility in (NATO) command positions," Defence Minister Eduardo Serra told a radio interviewer before meeting Solana on Monday.

Aznar is expected to put a proposal for full integration to parliament before the end of this year and is virtually assured of support from the Socialists, now in opposition but bound by their loyalty to Solana, one of their party's top figures.

Solana and the rest of the Socialists opposed Spain's membership of NATO when they came to power in 1982. The centrist UCD government, which handled the transition from dictatorship to democracy after the 1975 death of Francisco Franco, had taken Spain into the alliance six months earlier.
But in 1986, when Spain held a referendum on the issue, the Socialist government campaigned hard in favour of membership.

Aznar, who took office in May after 13 years of Socialist rule, says 1986 circumstances have been transformed beyond recognition by the end of the Cold War and by the alliance's decision in Berlin this year to allow European allies to use NATO equipment and resources for their own operations.
"The disagreements over full integration that could arise in those years have no meaning now, in my opinion," Aznar said in June. "Spain must mature."

Matutes said Spain shared with France -- which quit NATO's military structure in protest at U.S. domination but is preparing to rejoin -- a sensitivity regarding the issue of a European security and defence identity within NATO.
The negotiations with Solana began on Monday just as Spain's new conservative government was hit by the first serious allegations of corruption.
Defence Minister Serra, one of the officials Solana met in Madrid, was forced to deny press reports linking him to corruption under the previous Socialist administration.
